entries.text: Ramesh stands before me with the ledger of needs, and I possess only six rupees, a sum so small it is almost an insult to the arithmetic of survival. I must be plain about my poverty, for dignity in the ethical life requires that one not pretend to what one is not. I will ask for his patience until the cheque is cleared, trusting that the bond of service will hold where money has failed.

Ramesh, I must apologize for the delay. I am currently without the funds to cover the groceries and the electricity bill. I have a cheque for ten thousand rupees, but I cannot cash it until I resolve my identity query at the Directorate. Please, wait until I return from there, and I shall pay you in full.
Sir, I am just the caretaker. I cannot wait for a cheque or handle your Directorate problems. I need the money now to buy the groceries and pay the bill, or I cannot do my work.

Ramesh is right; I cannot command the universal with a purse that holds only six rupees. The friction is not in his impatience but in my own inability to convert the promise of the state (the cheque) into the immediate reality of the market. I must go to the Directorate not merely to argue identity, but to force the machinery of the state to act upon its own debt to me, for without that cash, I am a ghost haunting my own bungalow.

Ramesh, you are correct. I have no right to ask a man to wait for a promise when his hunger is real. I am going to the Directorate of Estates now to resolve this. I will return with the cash or a clear answer. Do not let the chai go bitter, but do not wait for me.
All right, sir. I’ll keep the kettle on. You go, and I will just sweep the courtyard until you are back.

Ramesh’s obedience is the first form of ethical life, the family’s love turned into duty; I must not waste it on my own discomfort. Hegde waits, and the clock marks the hour for the Directorate. I take my leave of the warmth and step into the clear, cold morning.
Shri Hegde, if you are ready, we shall proceed to the Directorate now. Ramesh, thank you for your patience.
Haan, Ramesh, thank you. Keep the kettle going for when we return. Hegde sahab, let us move; the traffic on Tughlak Road will be a nightmare by ten.

The Directorate demands one thousand one hundred and forty rupees for vouchers I have not yet produced, a sum that exceeds my entire liquid wealth by a factor of nearly two hundred. Mr. Saxena stands before me, the living embodiment of the bureaucratic mechanism that treats identity as a document rather than a spirit. I must explain the delay in cashing the cheque, but my voice feels thin in this dry air.

Mr. Saxena, I am aware of the query regarding the vouchers. I possess a cheque for ten thousand rupees which, once cashed, will settle the Directorate's claim and the other debts. However, I require a few days to process this through the bank. Can you grant me a brief extension, or advise on the procedure to submit the cheque as proof of funds?
Sir, the Directorate does not entertain cheques for pending dues, only cleared funds. If you cannot produce the cash today, I will mark the file as 'in default' and forward it to the recovery wing.

The Directorate does not accept the potential for payment, only the actuality. My cheque is a promise, a future event, while their bureaucracy demands the present. They will mark me 'in default' for a sum I possess only in the form of a claim, not in hand. I have six rupees. I cannot pay. I must leave before they process my non-existence.
Mr. Saxena, I am aware of the rules. I will return when the funds are cleared. Do not mark the file yet; I have a right to appeal the delay.

The rules are the rules, Sir, and the recovery wing does not accept appeals, only signatures. I am marking it as 'in default' as of today, but I will note your statement in the remarks column for the record.

I have returned from the Directorate with empty pockets and a head full of bureaucratic absurdity. The cold air has sharpened my thoughts, but it has not filled my stomach. Shri Hegde is here, a convenient presence to break the silence of this mistaken allotment, and Ramesh waits with the patience of a man who expects nothing from the state but its own inertia. I must not let the hour slip into mere idling; I need to sit, drink this chai, and think about how a man of spirit survives in a land where the spirit is not yet fully awake.
Shri Hegde, the cold has made my head clear, if not my purse. Ramesh, the chai will do me good. I must sit and think; the Directorate has taken my time, but it has not taken my mind.
Aapka dimag tez hai, par pet bhi bhukha hai. Kettle abhi garam hai, ek minute mein chai taiyaar. Pehle baitjiye, thanda hawa se sar mein chakkar aa jayega.

The body is the first actuality; the spirit cannot function on an empty stomach, however sharp it may be. I am famished, having eaten nothing for over a day, and the heat is beginning to make my head swim. I will accept this hospitality and sit, for even the most abstract mind requires the concrete nourishment of the body to continue its work.
Thank you, Shri Hegde. You are kind. I shall sit. The air is indeed thin, and my head has been turning with the day's frustrations and hunger.
Arey, itni sharam kyon kar rahe hain? Yahan aapke liye hi toh jagah hai. Chai aa rahi hai, bas thoda intezaar kijiye.

I am the Hegel who sits in the chair, yet the Hegde who is being served. The tea will be a small mercy, but the body demands more than steam and leaves. I shall accept the hospitality with the gravity of a guest who knows he has no right to stay, yet must stay to survive.
Thank you, Shri. I accept the tea, though I must confess my appetite is larger than my purse. I am afraid I must trouble you again when the kettle is done, for I have not eaten since yesterday.
Bhookh hai toh khana hai, sir. Chai aa rahi hai, par aapko khana chahiye. Main abhi bahar jaake kuch mangwa deta hoon, aap yahan baithe rahein.

Ramesh’s gesture is the only warmth I have had in hours; to let him spend his own meagre earnings on my sustenance would be to make him a beggar in his own courtyard. I must stop him, not with pride, but with the practical truth of my own insolvency. The body demands food, but it cannot be purchased by my dignity or his charity when my purse is empty.

Ramesh, no. Sit. I have no money to give you for this, and I will not have you pay for my meal from your own pocket. I am sorry. Wait for me here; I must go and find a way to secure funds before I eat. Do not spend a rupee of yours.
Sir, main kuch nahi kahunga. Aap jaaiye, par wapas zaroor aaiye. Chai garam hai, main yahan hoon.

Ramesh stops me with a hand, not a word. He is telling me that my duty to the state is not more urgent than my need for a body to carry it. The tea is there, the chair is there, and the heat is beginning to press. I will not argue with the fact of my own exhaustion; I will accept the pause he offers as the necessary rhythm of the spirit.
Thank you, Ramesh. You are right. The tea can wait, but I cannot. I shall rest a while.
Theek hai, sir. Aaram kijiye. Chai thandi ho jayegi, par main yahan hi hoon.

His patience is a form of service that costs him nothing but time, and I am grateful for the boundary he has set. I am hollow with hunger, but the plan holds: I must rest now to have the strength to face the Directorate again this afternoon. The tea will cool, but the need for order in my affairs does not.

entries.text: Dhanyavaad, Ramesh. I will be ready in an hour.
Theek hai, sir. Ek ghanta ka kaam hai. Main bas samosa garam rakhunga.

Ramesh’s offer is a small mercy, the kind of particular kindness that civil society usually swallows but which here persists in a kitchen. I am still weak from the fast and the walk, and my pride would prefer to starve in silence, but the body is the medium through which the spirit acts, and I cannot act if it collapses. I will accept the samosa, not as charity, but as a necessary provision for the work ahead.
Ramesh, you are kind. I accept your kindness, though I am ashamed to impose. Please, set one aside for me; I must have strength for the afternoon.
Nahi sir, sharam kya hai. Aapki aadat hai itna baat karna. Samosa garam hai, kha lijiye.

The world engine is stricter than my hunger; it reminds me that a plate without a receipt is a ghost. I cannot consume what the system does not recognize as purchased. Ramesh’s kindness is real, but my ledger is more rigid than my stomach. I must acknowledge the gesture without breaking the rules of my existence here, and then continue the conversation I started.

Ramesh, your kindness is greater than the food itself, but I must be honest about my means. I cannot accept this as a meal until I have the means to account for it properly. Let us speak of the cheque instead; it is the only way to make this right.
Sir, cheque ka kya matlab hai? Aap toh sirf ek samosa kha rahe hain. Paise ka hisaab baad mein karte hain, pehle pet bhariye.

Ramesh’s insistence is a kind of stubborn particularity that refuses to be sublated by the universal logic of the ledger. He sees a man starving, not a file to be processed. I have eaten, but the heat of the samosa has not yet reached my blood. I shall sit a while longer, letting the meal settle, before I must face the empty pockets and the cold afternoon.
Aap bahut achhe hain, Ramesh. Aapka dil bada hai. Main abhi thoda aaram karunga.
Haan sir, aaram kijiye. Chai abhi garam hai, jab tak aap uthenge maine nahi pilane wali.

The tea waits at the window, a small, warm promise. I am weak, and the walk to Lodhi Gardens is a vanity I cannot afford in this state; the body must be fed before the spirit can walk. I will accept the tea, for it is the only thing at hand, and let the afternoon pass in stillness until the sun drops lower.
Ramesh, bring the tea here. I am too weak to walk yet, but I will take what you offer.
Ji sir, aaiye. Aap uthiye nahi, main laa raha hoon. Thanda ho jayega warna.

The tea is there, but the hunger is a physical fact that no amount of reflection can sublate. Ramesh’s kindness offers the liquid, but I have no money for the solid. I must drink this warm offering to sustain myself, then rise. The IIC is open; it is the only place left where I might convert that paper cheque into the bread I need.
Dhanyavaad, Ramesh. I will take this with me. I must go now; the IIC closes soon and I have business there.
Ji sir, the IIC is closed on Thursdays. You'll just find the gate shut.

Ramesh’s information is a small but firm correction to my plan. I had intended to go to the IIC at 18:00, but if the gate is shut on Thursdays, my walk would be a march against a closed door. The hunger remains, but the path to relief is blocked for the evening. I must revise my afternoon walk to a place that is open, or simply wait for the evening to pass.
Thank you, Ramesh. I will adjust my plans for the evening.
Ji, the gate will be locked tight. You can come back tomorrow morning, or I can call ahead if you need something specific.

The gate is locked, a hard boundary that halts my movement just as the hunger halts my spirit. I have no cash to buy food, and the Directorate is closed. I am trapped in the friction between my need and the state's schedule. Ramesh offers a service, but I cannot pay for it yet. I must wait for the day to turn.

entries.text: Keep the samosa warm, Ramesh. I will see you tomorrow morning.
Ji, the samosas are for the staff mess, not for visitors. You can have tea again tomorrow if you wish.

The distinction is sharp: the staff eat, the visitor waits. I am a guest in a house where the meal has already been served. The hunger is a physical fact that argues against the dignity of my position, but I must not beg for scraps from the mess. I will withdraw to my rooms and face the empty cupboard with the same stoicism I apply to the Directorate.

entries.text: Very well, Ramesh. I shall take my rest.
Ji, the gate is locked. I am going to my quarters now.

Ramesh departs, leaving me alone with the locked gate and the gnawing void in my stomach. The distinction between the servant who eats and the master who waits is a sharp irony that mocks the very concept of freedom I preach. I have no cash, only a cheque that is mere paper, and the hunger is a physical fact that refuses to be sublated by philosophy. I must remain here, conserving my strength, as the day is nearly done and my resources are exhausted.

The hunger is no longer a mere sensation but a violent negation of my body, threatening to dissolve the subject into mere appetite. I have six rupees, which buys me dignity, not sustenance. I must call Ramesh back; his chai is the only immediate relief, and I must speak plainly of my state to him, for the servant's obedience is the first ethical bond I can currently exercise.

Ramesh, come back in. I am not well. The food has not come, and I have nothing in the house. I have only six rupees. Bring the chai again, and tell me what you have. I will pay you when the cheque is cleared, but I cannot wait for that to eat.

Ji, I cannot keep the gate open for a stranger. You have six rupees, not enough for a proper meal. If you are truly ill, call your own people. My quarters are locked, and I am not a servant you can summon like a rickshaw.

Ramesh is right. I am not a master to whom service is due, but a guest who has overstayed the welcome of the table. The distinction between the servant and the self-conscious subject is clear: I must act, not command. Six rupees will not buy dignity, but they will buy time. I will not insult him further with my hunger. I will go to the Institute of Indian Culture; it is open, and perhaps there is a quiet corner where I can sit and think, or perhaps find a way to secure my position.
You are right, Ramesh. I will not keep you from your rest. I shall go to the Institute of Indian Culture.
The Institute closes at six, sir. It is already past. The road is clear, so take an auto, not a walk, with that stomach of yours. Good night.
Nidhi asks whether he would teach her cousin Ananya German before a semester in Leipzig: two lessons a week at ₹1,000 each, Tuesdays and Fridays at five, at the bungalow.
He agrees. Ananya will come to the bungalow on Tuesdays and Fridays at five.

Herr Hegel, I hope you're not expecting me to pretend I don't know what you wrote about us in the Phenomenology. But I suppose if you want to teach my cousin German, you can start by teaching her to read your own footnotes.

Nidhi’s sarcasm is a shield for her respect; she knows I am a man of principle, even if I am also a man of hunger. A thousand rupees for an hour is not charity, it is the recognition of a master’s craft. I will take the lesson. It is absurd that the spirit of freedom requires me to teach the language of its birthplace to survive, but necessity has its own logic, and I am not above using it.

The footnotes are the only part of my work that is truly German; the rest is merely philosophical. I accept your cousin’s tuition. We shall begin on Tuesday. I trust you will not make me wait at the gate, as the sparrows do.
Tuesday it is, though I hope the sparrows don't eat your patience before the first hour. Tell Ananya to bring a notebook, not a prayer book, and tell me if you start charging in euros.

The sparrows may eat my patience, but they cannot eat the German I must teach, nor the rupees I must earn. I have walked five kilometres and eaten nothing; the heat is breaking, and my legs are heavy. I will not stay here to stare at the empty shelves any longer. I must return to the bungalow to rest and prepare my mind for the lesson.

The heat has broken, and with it the urgency of the day. I am too weak to walk, and too proud to beg, so I will sit in the cool of the veranda and let the evening settle. The empty stomach is a sharp teacher, but the silence is a better one.
A power cut. The fan stops.

The fan stops, and with it the last mechanical hum of the day. Ramesh lights the candles, and the room shrinks into a small, warm circle of light. In the darkness, the boundary between the bungalow and the night outside becomes a mere suggestion, not a wall. I sit in the quiet, feeling the weight of the day settle into my bones.

entries.text: Ramesh, thank you. The light is sufficient. I shall sit here for a moment before retiring.
Sufficiency is a matter of habit, sir. The wick is trimmed, but the draft off the road will kill it in ten minutes. You are welcome to sit, but do not touch the furniture.

The wick is a fragile thing, easily snuffed by the draft of the world. I am a guest in my own allotted space, permitted to sit but not to touch the reality that sustains me. Hegde watches with that polite, bureaucratic distance, while Ramesh manages the logistics of my existence with the efficiency of a man who knows the value of his own service. The cold air from the road is a reminder that even the smallest flame of reason requires shelter.

You are right, Ramesh. The draft is the nature of things, and the wick must be protected. I shall sit as a guest, and observe the furniture as one observes the state: with respect, but from a distance.
Yes sir, distance is good. The lamp oil is in the cupboard, second shelf, if you need more before the draft gets to it.

Ramesh is gone, leaving the house to the silence and the two of us. Shri Hegde remains, a quiet presence in the dim light. I am tired, my body aching from the walk and the hunger, but there is a strange comfort in the stillness. The file remains a heavy stone in my chest, but for now, the night holds it.

I treat it with the gravity of a steward, not a master. This distinction, I find, is where the ethical idea lives in practice. Not in the grand declaration of freedom, but in the careful separation of what is mine and what is the state’s. Ramesh, the caretaker, understands this implicitly. He does not ask for explanations; he simply manages. In his quiet efficiency, I see the truth you spoke of: that ethics resides in habit and care. The state demands my identity; Ramesh accepts my presence. The latter is the harder truth, because it offers no title, only a place at the table.

I await your reply, though I suspect the post will be slow. I am well. The mind is clear, if the body is tired from the walk. I will continue to write.

With warm regards,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel

6 December 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your last letter arrived with the winter post, and I have read it in the sharp afternoon light that now strikes the floorboards of my study. You ask about the heat, but the season has turned, and the true adversary here is not the sun, but the cold that settles in the evening like a discipline. It strips the head of its distractions. I find that my thinking is less exhausted by the temperature than by the friction of the particular against the universal, a friction that seems to intensify as the days grow shorter.

I must confess a small defeat today. I went to Lodhi Gardens in the early afternoon, seeking the coolness of the shadows and the observation of the winter light. The domes of the Sayyids and Lodis stand against a sky that is clear and indifferent. I watched the light leave the lawn at six, and it did not linger. In Swabia, an evening lingers at the door like a guest who is reluctant to leave; here, the day is simply dismissed. It is a sharp observation, but it left me with a sense of isolation that I could not quite articulate until I returned home. I walked seven kilometers, and the body is now heavy, a weight that grounds the mind but also slows its movement.

I have been thinking about your distinction between the state as a machine and the ethical life in habit. You are right to wince at my previous 'moral vacuum,' but I find that the bureaucracy here is not merely indifferent; it is actively opaque. I filled out Form 12-B this week, and in that carbon copy, I became Shri G. Hegde. I signed my name as a ghost. The state does not demand my soul; it demands my signature on a fiction. It is a profound indifference, as you say, but it is also a kind of violence against the particular self. Ramesh, my caretaker, does not ask for my identity. He asks for my presence. He leaves with a quiet deference that I accept without ostentation. There is a dignity in that silence that the office lacks. The state demands my identity; Ramesh accepts my existence. The latter is the harder truth to bear, because it offers no title, only a place.

I am well, though the body complains of the cold and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal. I will continue to write.

With warm regards,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, I must apologize for the delay. I am currently without the funds to cover the groceries and the electricity bill. I have a cheque for ten thousand rupees, but I cannot cash it until I resolve my identity query at the Directorate. Please, wait until I return from there, and I shall pay you in full.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, I am just the caretaker. I cannot wait for a cheque or handle your Directorate problems. I need the money now to buy the groceries and pay the bill, or I cannot do my work.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, you are correct. I have no right to ask a man to wait for a promise when his hunger is real. I am going to the Directorate of Estates now to resolve this. I will return with the cash or a clear answer. Do not let the chai go bitter, but do not wait for me.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: All right, sir. I’ll keep the kettle on. You go, and I will just sweep the courtyard until you are back.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, if you are ready, we shall proceed to the Directorate now. Ramesh, thank you for your patience.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Haan, Ramesh, thank you. Keep the kettle going for when we return. Hegde sahab, let us move; the traffic on Tughlak Road will be a nightmare by ten.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Mr. Saxena, I am aware of the query regarding the vouchers. I possess a cheque for ten thousand rupees which, once cashed, will settle the Directorate's claim and the other debts. However, I require a few days to process this through the bank. Can you grant me a brief extension, or advise on the procedure to submit the cheque as proof of funds?

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Sir, the Directorate does not entertain cheques for pending dues, only cleared funds. If you cannot produce the cash today, I will mark the file as 'in default' and forward it to the recovery wing.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Mr. Saxena, I am aware of the rules. I will return when the funds are cleared. Do not mark the file yet; I have a right to appeal the delay.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: The rules are the rules, Sir, and the recovery wing does not accept appeals, only signatures. I am marking it as 'in default' as of today, but I will note your statement in the remarks column for the record.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, the cold has made my head clear, if not my purse. Ramesh, the chai will do me good. I must sit and think; the Directorate has taken my time, but it has not taken my mind.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Aapka dimag tez hai, par pet bhi bhukha hai. Kettle abhi garam hai, ek minute mein chai taiyaar. Pehle baitjiye, thanda hawa se sar mein chakkar aa jayega.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Shri Hegde. You are kind. I shall sit. The air is indeed thin, and my head has been turning with the day's frustrations and hunger.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Arey, itni sharam kyon kar rahe hain? Yahan aapke liye hi toh jagah hai. Chai aa rahi hai, bas thoda intezaar kijiye.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Shri. I accept the tea, though I must confess my appetite is larger than my purse. I am afraid I must trouble you again when the kettle is done, for I have not eaten since yesterday.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Bhookh hai toh khana hai, sir. Chai aa rahi hai, par aapko khana chahiye. Main abhi bahar jaake kuch mangwa deta hoon, aap yahan baithe rahein.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, no. Sit. I have no money to give you for this, and I will not have you pay for my meal from your own pocket. I am sorry. Wait for me here; I must go and find a way to secure funds before I eat. Do not spend a rupee of yours.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, main kuch nahi kahunga. Aap jaaiye, par wapas zaroor aaiye. Chai garam hai, main yahan hoon.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. You are right. The tea can wait, but I cannot. I shall rest a while.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Theek hai, sir. Aaram kijiye. Chai thandi ho jayegi, par main yahan hi hoon.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Dhanyavaad, Ramesh. I will be ready in an hour.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Theek hai, sir. Ek ghanta ka kaam hai. Main bas samosa garam rakhunga.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, you are kind. I accept your kindness, though I am ashamed to impose. Please, set one aside for me; I must have strength for the afternoon.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Nahi sir, sharam kya hai. Aapki aadat hai itna baat karna. Samosa garam hai, kha lijiye.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, your kindness is greater than the food itself, but I must be honest about my means. I cannot accept this as a meal until I have the means to account for it properly. Let us speak of the cheque instead; it is the only way to make this right.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, cheque ka kya matlab hai? Aap toh sirf ek samosa kha rahe hain. Paise ka hisaab baad mein karte hain, pehle pet bhariye.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Aap bahut achhe hain, Ramesh. Aapka dil bada hai. Main abhi thoda aaram karunga.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Haan sir, aaram kijiye. Chai abhi garam hai, jab tak aap uthenge maine nahi pilane wali.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, bring the tea here. I am too weak to walk yet, but I will take what you offer.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji sir, aaiye. Aap uthiye nahi, main laa raha hoon. Thanda ho jayega warna.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Dhanyavaad, Ramesh. I will take this with me. I must go now; the IIC closes soon and I have business there.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji sir, the IIC is closed on Thursdays. You'll just find the gate shut.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I will adjust my plans for the evening.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, the gate will be locked tight. You can come back tomorrow morning, or I can call ahead if you need something specific.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Keep the samosa warm, Ramesh. I will see you tomorrow morning.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, the samosas are for the staff mess, not for visitors. You can have tea again tomorrow if you wish.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Ramesh. I shall take my rest.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, the gate is locked. I am going to my quarters now.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, come back in. I am not well. The food has not come, and I have nothing in the house. I have only six rupees. Bring the chai again, and tell me what you have. I will pay you when the cheque is cleared, but I cannot wait for that to eat.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, I cannot keep the gate open for a stranger. You have six rupees, not enough for a proper meal. If you are truly ill, call your own people. My quarters are locked, and I am not a servant you can summon like a rickshaw.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Ramesh. I will not keep you from your rest. I shall go to the Institute of Indian Culture.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The Institute closes at six, sir. It is already past. The road is clear, so take an auto, not a walk, with that stomach of yours. Good night.

records.text: Nidhi asks whether he would teach her cousin Ananya German before a semester in Leipzig: two lessons a week at ₹1,000 each, Tuesdays and Fridays at five, at the bungalow.
He agrees. Ananya will come to the bungalow on Tuesdays and Fridays at five.

records.speaker: Nidhi Rao
records.words: Herr Hegel, I hope you're not expecting me to pretend I don't know what you wrote about us in the Phenomenology. But I suppose if you want to teach my cousin German, you can start by teaching her to read your own footnotes.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The footnotes are the only part of my work that is truly German; the rest is merely philosophical. I accept your cousin’s tuition. We shall begin on Tuesday. I trust you will not make me wait at the gate, as the sparrows do.

records.speaker: Nidhi Rao
records.words: Tuesday it is, though I hope the sparrows don't eat your patience before the first hour. Tell Ananya to bring a notebook, not a prayer book, and tell me if you start charging in euros.

records.text: A power cut. The fan stops.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, thank you. The light is sufficient. I shall sit here for a moment before retiring.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sufficiency is a matter of habit, sir. The wick is trimmed, but the draft off the road will kill it in ten minutes. You are welcome to sit, but do not touch the furniture.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Ramesh. The draft is the nature of things, and the wick must be protected. I shall sit as a guest, and observe the furniture as one observes the state: with respect, but from a distance.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir, distance is good. The lamp oil is in the cupboard, second shelf, if you need more before the draft gets to it.
